chapter: The craft of the ad lib player
title: Bass players, drummers and the lost show-business workshop
summary: Hall says today's drummers lack the experience of accompanying show acts, and bass and drums must team together.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x:
How about drummers? Bass players
and drummers, you know, they're always allied very closely,
and there's always been, you know, on one hand a very tight
knit thing; on the other hand, there can be a friction.

Well, the drummers of today, there are
several fine drummers of today, say, Jackie Williams or
Connie
Tommy Kay, or Red Baer. There are so many I couldn't even

think of, but the drummers of today didn't get the experience of the early years of show business, because the drummers had to play for dance groups, chorus girls, et cetera, performers that required special effects, and the young drummers of the day hadn't -- didn't have that workshop to rely on.

Big Sid Catlett and O'Neill Spencer, Kaiser Marshall and those kind of people were -- the chorus girls would love to see them in the band because they'd know there was going to be a fine performance. But the young -- young guys, they're all individualists. They go in for gimmickry more than to be a part of a section.

That's when the bass players and drummers were inseparable. They had to team together like saxophones and OR trumpets. And once one guy got out of his, out of the realm of his being with the group, then you wouldn't have a regular, steady beat.
But sometimes, you know, you can always have two fine instrumentalists, a drummer and a bass player, but together they -- they just don't, you know, mesh.
